chapter: With Benny Goodman and Louis Armstrong
title: Macon: the Krupa trumpeter beaten by military police for speaking to Simmons and Sid
summary: A white soldier-trumpeter coming to see Simmons and Sid was beaten by police and MPs; years later he explains how it ended.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: All right, we had a -- I hate this, why can't you just say people, instead of Caucasian or white or colored or black? We had an audience in the balcony and it was a black dance, so you know who the audience was, right? But if it

had sounded too good, they would have taken over. So at the end of the dance, the band valet, his name was Mutt, came back and said, "John, you and Sid. There's a soldier out here that wants to see you all. Say you are the only two in the band he know." I say, "Yeah," well, I was dressed, I'd changed. Sid was still standing there, soaking wet. He was trying to dry off, cool off and everything.

I said, "Sid, I'm going to go across the street and get some cigarettes and Pepsi, and I'll see who it is." And I get outside the dressing room, and I see a friend of mine from Gene Krupa's band. By name of [Murphy DeFono] He had a jet black hair with a lock hanging up front, you know, nice looking guy. Trumpet player. Now,he hadn't had any Army training, boot training at all. He was in the band. Here comes this Macon, Georgia policeman, with his jeans on, his cowboy boots, and his hog leg hanging down -- hog leg, you know, handgun, hanging down to his knee, Boston Stetson hat. "Where you going, boy?" Talking to Murphy. Said, "I'm going back here to see John and Sid. They're friends of mine." "You got to get out of here and put some charcoal on your face first." And he shook him down and found some whisky on him. Got the whisky bottle in his hand. Well, I followed them on out. And he turned him over to the M.P.'s. Right there on the triangle. The M.P.s beat hell out of him. They beat him so he urinated on himself. And something else, I guess. The city police joined in, with

billy clubs. "You Yankee son of a bitch. Didn't we tell you not to speak to no niggers down here?" "But they're friends of mine." Whop, whop, whop. He was adding to the injury, you know. And they almost killed him.

So he has one of these native girls, with my paint job. "Boy, why don't you go on away from here. You ain't doing nothing but causing trouble." Well, this brings me to my senses. Naturally, I'm next. So I went on across the street and got the Pepsi-Cola and the cigarettes, and went around the triangle, you know. And went back inside and said, "Man, they're beating hell out of that man out there."

They took him out of the band, and put him in the infantry. Without any boot training at all. So he got to Paris, and started drinking. And somehow, he struck up a conversation with some Sengalese soldiers. Well, and they said words to the effect of, "it seems like you got a problem," or "you're afraid to fight, or what?" And he ran the story down to them, you know, he says, "I don't know nothing about fighting. Never had a gun in my hand, you know?" And the conversation went on and on, told them about the M.P.s, and the commanding officer, whatnot. So about a year later, I ran into Murphy on Broadway, there by that amusement place on 52nd and Broadway, where they have all these little gadgets you can peep through and tricks and things.
I ran into him on that corner. "Murphy." "John."

I said, "Man, the last time, you looked a mess, all on our account." He said, "No, it wasn't on your account. It was on account of my bullheadedness," he said, "and forgetting where I was." I say, "Well, how did you make it through the Army?" He say, "I got put back in the band." I say, "Well, what happened?" He say, "Well, the M.P.s and commanding officer came up missing in action." He said, "And when they called my number, I told the new C.O. my problem, you know, that I had never fired a gun or anything. I was in the band and everything, what had happened. So he put me back in the band. So everything came out all right after all." He say, "I don't know what happened to them," he say, "but I had planned something for them anyway."
After the Army, did he go back to playing?

Yes, he went back and rejoined Gene Krupa. And it was very good to see him, you know. It took a lot of -- how shall we say -- blame off my shoulders, because I really felt that it was Sid and my fault, you know. 'Cause if we hadn't of been there, he wouldn't have been there. You know, that's one way of looking at it.
